newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Br. Steel seen tightening grip on Avesta Sheffield.
newsitem.headline: Br. Steel seen tightening grip on Avesta Sheffield.

text.p: Swedish/British steel producer Avesta Sheffield posted a poor result for the first half of 1996/97 on Friday and announced a leadership change that takes it further into the fold of parent company British Steel Plc.
Avesta posted a pre-tax profit of 24 million crowns ($3.63 million) for the six months to September 30 compared to 2.29 billion crowns in the same period a year ago.

"A loss of 204 million crowns was incurred in the second quarter as a result of very low sales prices and with a heavy influence of price changes in inventory of minus 182 million crowns," the company said in a statement.
Analysts said the result was below the market forecast for a pre-tax profit of 169 million crowns but looked worse on paper because of the larger-than-expected drop in stock value.
"But everything was adverse in the second quarter," said UBS analyst Peter Dupont.
As well as inventory losses, prices fell and the result was hit by commissioning problems at the Avesta melt shop and Nyby cold mill.
The stronger Swedish crown wiped 100 million crowns off six month sales which tumbled 25 percent to 8.42 billion crowns.
"But the situation should get better over the balance of the year and next year and 1997/98 could be a reasonable year," Dupont told Reuters.
Analysts said the report did have a modestly positive tone, saying that prices have starting to pick up against after slumping to a low in July/August.
"Further increases are expected but it is uncertain at what pace they will be achieved," the company said.
"The group, rather than relying on improving external conditions, is putting priority focus on measures to improve cost efficiency and realise the full benefits of its completed investments."
Avesta Sheffield shares closed unchanged on the Stockholm bourse at 65 crowns.

But the market was surprised by the announcement that chief executive officer Per Molin will step down in June 1997 and be replaced by Stuart Pettifor, current head of the plates, and commercial steel division of parent company British Steel.
To date the company, that was formed by a merger between Sweden's Avesta and Britain's Sheffield, has always had a Swedish chief executive but British chairman.
Both position will now be held by Britons.
"Avesta Sheffield will be looking even more like just a subsidiary of British Steel and not a Swedish company," said analyst Christofer Sjogren from Carnegie.
"I think this will fuel speculation about another takeover or increase in British control on the company."

In July this year British Steel declined to comment on newspaper reports that it was looking to take 100 percent control of the stainless steel group that has operations in Britain, Sweden and North America.
Last year British Steel increased its holding in Avesta Sheffield to 51 percent from 49.9 percent.
"My assumption has always been that British Steel will buy it out and they will put their own man in," Dupont said.
"This is broadly consistent with that."
